papers.title: The Elephant-Goldfish Model for software design review: what a fresh reviewer can see
papers.abstract: A design can be easy to understand and still specify the wrong system. Google's Elephant-Goldfish Model asks fresh agents to review a design without the conversation that produced it. We examined how this choice affects detection of omissions, agreement violations and internal defects. We seeded nine defects in each of 47 public software design documents and supplied each with a scripted drafting conversation. A fresh reviewer given the conversation as its own earlier exchange detected 94.8% of omitted-decision instances, compared with 62.4% for the same model given the document alone. It detected 98.3% of violations of conversation-only requirements. On document-visible defects, recall was 87.5% with the conversation and 88.4% without it, equivalent within a prespecified 15-percentage-point margin. Three model judges scored detection and were calibrated on constructed controls. In document-only runs, the plugin's five-stage review took a geometric mean of 9.03 minutes against 1.81 for one reviewer. Its estimated recall was lower under both judging procedures, with a difference distinguishable from zero under one. A later generic-prompt comparison gave a similar result. The experiment separates two objectives for automated design review: testing whether a new reader can reconstruct the design and checking whether the design preserves the decisions that govern implementation.

papers.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
papers.abstract: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

papers.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

papers.title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

papers.title: The AMPEL Platform: A Concept for Open-Source Collaboration in Developing In-House Medical Device Software under EU-Regulation
papers.abstract: Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) are expected to enhance medical treatment through automated data analysis, yet a substantial evidence gap persists as to whether they actually improve patient outcomes. It arises due to the black-box nature of commercial products and the constrains of the European medical device regulation (MDR) for such studies: patient outcomes may only be collected through the use of medical device software (MDSW). In-house MDSW under Article 5(5) MDR is a promising solution, allowing healthcare facilities to manufacture and study such software for their own use under reduced requirements. However, the overall limited experience with in-house MDSW development in Europe currently restricts the widespread use of this regulatory approach. While open-source software generally fosters evidence generation, publishing an in-house MDSW as open source would risk a classification as "placement on the market", which the MDR prohibits. The concept presented here builds on experience from developing an in-house CDSS at the University of Leipzig Medical Center, expert discussions, a literature review and a formal legal opinion. A companion online wiki summarizes and regularly updates the results. The current concept outlines a shared open-source codebase, which doesn't constitute a medical device under the MDR. Also, "Data Input" modules must be programmed separately at each site, while still allowing for multicenter collaboration on the codebase. Atypically for open-source projects, this leaves a considerable effort to deploy the software within each site, e.g. each healthcare facility must independently meet the MDR requirements for an in-house MDSW. The AMPEL concept describes a regulatory pathway for the open-source publication and development of in-house MDSW. It underpins the open-source AMPEL platform, which helps healthcare facilities build their own in-house CDSS.

papers.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

papers.title: Software-Engineering-as-an-Artifact: From Engines to Systems That Build Themselves
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SE) is evolving rapidly as generative AI and LLM-based agents grow more capable. Yet, as a community, we risk using these new tools to solve problems that a changing SE process may no longer pose. We consider how AI may transform, and in part already is transforming, both the SE process and the systems it produces. Drawing on scenario planning methods from futures studies, we extrapolate from observed trends to a deliberately extreme scenario in which the SE process fully materializes in artifacts (like context documentation and executable skills). Such a process would culminate in SE engines that autonomously produce and update systems directly from requirements and user requests. The work of human engineers would then shift from the product to the process: they would maintain the artifacts of these engines, while the engines produce and evolve the software. We probe this scenario in scenario-validation interviews with four SE industry practitioners. The interviewees found the scenario largely plausible and desirable, and two reported that parts of industry are already moving this way; one questioned whether tacit engineering knowledge can ever be fully captured in artifacts. Even if this end state is reached only in part, we argue that reasoning about it can inform the intermediate stages. SE research should therefore take such futures into account when choosing its research directions.

papers.title: EdgeALM: An Efficient and Unified Edge Accelerator for Large Audio Language Models via Full-Stack Hardware-Software Co-Design and Agent-Driven Recursive Optimization
papers.abstract: Edge deployment of audio language models (ALMs) is constrained by large model footprints, heterogeneous workloads, and limited software support. This paper presents EdgeALM, an efficient and unified FPGA accelerator for ALMs that combines full-stack hardware-software co-design with agent-driven recursive optimization. An end-to-end ALM compression flow is developed, combining a unified AWQ-style quantizer with modality-conditioned vocabulary pruning. A Conv-Matmul Disaggregation architecture is proposed, with dedicated matrix and convolution engines that operate concurrently on their respective workloads. An Extra-Coarse-Grained ISA is designed to incorporate regular on-chip data movement and execution sequences into compute instructions, reducing software complexity with modest hardware control overhead. Hardware and software recursive loops are introduced for agent-driven full-stack optimization. The proposed EdgeALM is implemented on a single Alveo U50 in an ordinary desktop PC and demonstrates inference on more than 20 models, including ALMs with up to 13B parameters within the 8-GB HBM capacity. It achieves high-throughput audio-to-text inference at up to 169.5 tokens/s and sustains real-time streaming audio-to-audio inference, with 94% bandwidth utilization and 26 W power consumption on average. Standalone ASR, text-only LLM, and TTS models are also well supported, and can be combined in cascades. Compared with state-of-the-art FPGA accelerators (e.g., EdgeLLM), EdgeALM scales to larger models and supports a wider range of inference workloads extended to the audio modality, while achieving higher bandwidth utilization at lower board power and cost.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
papers.abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

papers.title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.

papers.title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
papers.abstract: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.

papers.title: Implementation and Software-in-the-Loop Evaluation of a Trans-Domain Digital Twin Architecture for Autonomous Guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV Without Online GNSS
papers.abstract: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or unreliable in enclosed spaces, blind spots caused by natural obstacles and structures, and environments affected by radio interference and signal spoofing during electronic warfare. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a system based on a Trans-Domain Digital Twin (TDDT) for autonomous guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV. Independent navigation, flight dynamics, and meteorological models are coordinated within a cycle of state estimation, prediction, decision-making, command execution, and feedback. Data from inertial, magnetic, pressure, and airspeed sensors, together with environmental information, form the basis for estimation and prediction. Furthermore, a shared state, temporal synchronization, preservation of information provenance, and command traceability establish continuity between models and decisions. The system was tested with a simulated physical twin in a software-in-the-loop environment. Vertical takeoff, movement toward the destination, landing, and autonomous stopping were recorded, and the dynamic model was adjusted to a limited extent based on sensor-derived feedback. Separating the evaluation reference from navigation inputs enabled independent assessment of positioning error and computational performance. The results confirm operational coordination, decision traceability, and closed-loop guidance under the tested conditions, providing a reproducible platform for the development and evaluation of navigation without satellite-based positioning.

papers.title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

papers.title: VEGA: A Scalable Software-Hardware Co-design for Genome Alignment using RVV Extension
papers.abstract: Dynamic programming (DP)-based genome sequence analysis is fundamental to computational genomics, but it remains computationally intensive as genomic data volumes continue to outpace Moore's Law. Existing hardware accelerators often sacrifice programmability and scalability across diverse alignment algorithms. In this work, we present VEGA, a scalable software-hardware co-design that accelerates genome alignment using RISC-V Vector extensions. VEGA introduces specialized vector instructions and three key innovations: a Forefront Stationary dataflow that minimizes off-chip memory access, intersequence parallelism that maximizes SIMD lane utilization, and custom ISA extensions that accelerate core alignment operations. Evaluations show that VEGA achieves up to 15.1x and 9.7x speedups for Edit Distance and Smith-Waterman algorithms over the Ara2-RVV vector baseline, sustaining 10.2x and 6.7x gains for 10kbp sequences. Post-synthesis results indicate only 1.0% area overhead compared to a standard RISC-V core, with performance-per-area efficiency rivaling specialized ASICs. VEGA thus achieves a balanced advancement in efficiency, programmability, and scalability for genome sequence alignment.

papers.title: Perceived Differences in Activity and Experience Between Developing Software With and Without AI
papers.abstract: The fundamental changes in software engineering driven by generative AI will have profound effects not only on the number of available software engineering jobs but also on what software engineering itself looks like. As the career evolves, questions arise about what the skillset and interests of the next generation of software engineers will be and whether long-time engineers will continue to be attracted to the career. In this paper, we contribute to answering these questions by studying how software development with AI tools is perceived to differ from traditional development and how the differences are modulated by years of programming experience. We find that, in terms of programming activities, engineers report less talking with peers about technical problems, less decomposition, less searching of documentation, and less using a debugger, while they report more task switching. We also find experiential differences, including less deep focus and less sense of control over code and design. We call these the different craft results, in contrast to core code-production activities such as writing, refactoring, and fixing code, which show only small mean differences. We also find that these differences are amplified by years of programming experience (an experience gradient), with software engineers who started programming before the age of generative AI perceiving greater changes in both activity and developer experience. We discuss our findings and their implications on training of the next generation of engineers and on engineers who may have difficulty transitioning to the AI-infused world of software engineering.

papers.title: From 6G Capabilities to Software-Business Value: A Multivocal Review of Characteristics, Opportunities, Challenges
papers.abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) technology is expected to enable intelligent, autonomous, and software-defined ecosystems, creating new ways for software firms to generate value. However, evidence on the characteristics, opportunities, and challenges of 6G software businesses remains fragmented across academic and practitioner literature. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 133 sources (102 peer-reviewed studies and 31 grey literature sources) to examine this emerging landscape from the perspective of software-producing organizations. Thematic analysis identified 18 characteristics grouped into five themes, 32 business opportunities across eight themes, and 19 challenges and constraints across six themes. Three independent raters assessed the reliability of factor-to-theme classification, with Fleiss' kappa indicating substantial to almost perfect agreement (0.744 to 0.832). Findings suggest that value creation depends not only on technological capabilities but also on translating them into viable services and business models while addressing integration complexity, organizational and economic barriers, regulatory uncertainty, and security and sustainability concerns. The synthesis reveals that characteristics, opportunities, and challenges are interdependent dimensions of 6G software businesses. By integrating academic and practitioner evidence, this study provides a traceable foundation for future empirical research and strategic decision-making as 6G technologies, standards, and markets evolve.

papers.title: Stratum: A Hardware-Software Co-Design Framework for SNN Inference on RISC-V
papers.abstract: Efficient spiking neural network (SNN) inference on RISC-V processors requires tracing implementation costs back to the compiler and hardware decisions that produce them. Training environments, compilers, and cycle-level simulators, however, typically operate as distinct tools, making this attribution difficult. This paper presents Stratum, a framework that integrates an snnTorch-trained SNN, an MLIR-based compiler stack, and a cycle-level gem5-based RISC-V model into a unified workflow. Stratum exposes two optimization levers, software decisions in the generated code and hardware configuration choices in the simulated core, and uses stage-level cycle measurements to identify performance bottlenecks. We demonstrate Stratum on a two-layer N-MNIST network with three controlled comparisons: (i)~dense vs.\ spike-gated lowering of \texttt{snn.linear}, (ii)~output-outer vs.\ spike-major weight layout with spike-gating enabled in both binaries, and (iii)~L2 cache capacity with both layouts. Our spike-gated lowering reduces simulated inference time by $64\times$ (453.2\,ms to 7.04\,ms), and our spike-major layout cuts it by a further 37.2\% (to 4.42\,ms) at 4\,MiB L2, with the predicted class unchanged. The layout speedup grows from $1.59\times$ to $1.88\times$ when L2 shrinks to 1\,MiB. These results show that Stratum enables rapid early evaluation of design choices at both the software level (compiler stack) and the hardware level (cycle-level gem5 simulation).

papers.title: Simulation-Based Testing of RCM-Constrained Robotic Software via Task Manifolds
papers.abstract: System-level testing of surgical robots requires generating executable test scenarios that exercise diverse, safety-critical behaviors. However, remote-center-of-motion (RCM) surgical manipulators operate within tightly constrained workspaces governed by coupled task geometry, inverse kinematics, and motor limits. Direct sampling in motor-command or Cartesian spaces frequently wastes testing budgets on physically unfeasible configurations. To address this limitation, we present a manifold-centered testing framework that decouples feasible test-domain construction from downstream test-generation strategies. Candidate inputs are generated directly within this constructed feasible domain and mapped to lower-level joint commands for simulation execution. Offline trajectory safety oracles and a spatial reference grid then evaluate failure yield and coverage. We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies. Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage. Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics. Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.

papers.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
papers.abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

papers.title: Impact of Edge Software Evolution on Audio Tagging Models: An Empirical Study on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
papers.abstract: Audio tagging is a fundamental task in machine listening, enabling the automatic identification of acoustic events in applications such as intelligent monitoring, industrial inspection, environmental sensing, and smart environments. As these applications increasingly migrate to edge platforms, deployment-oriented metrics such as latency, energy consumption, and resource utilization become critical alongside predictive performance. However, most existing studies evaluate audio tagging models under a single software environment, overlooking the potential impact of software stack evolution on deployment efficiency. This paper investigates how software ecosystem updates affect the execution characteristics of state-of-the-art audio tagging architectures on edge devices. We evaluate representative convolutional and Transformer-based models, including PANNs (CNN and ResNet variants), AST, and PaSST, on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano platform using two generations of NVIDIA's software ecosystem: JetPack 6.2 and JetPack 7.2. Under identical hardware conditions, we analyze inference latency, energy consumption, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory footprint across multiple inference backends and power modes. The results show that software stack evolution can substantially affect deployment performance. JetPack 7.2 reduces latency and energy consumption by more than 50% for several convolutional architectures when combined with TensorRT, while significantly increasing GPU utilization. In contrast, AST exhibits only marginal gains, whereas PaSST shows intermediate behavior. These findings demonstrate that software evolution is a critical factor in Edge AI evaluation and can alter the relative deployment efficiency of competing architectures. Consequently, software stack versions should be explicitly considered when benchmarking and selecting audio tagging models for embedded deployment.

papers.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

papers.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
papers.abstract: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.

papers.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
papers.abstract: Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.

papers.title: Software-Defined Internet Integration of Satellite Networks (SDISN)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes SDISN, a software-defined Internet integration of satellite networks. It facilitates the transmission of IP traffic from user terminals (UTs) or Internet nodes over a satellite network with inter-satellite links (ISLs). Gateways (GWs) together with Points of Presence (PoPs) support the transition between the satellite network and the Internet. UTs and GWs connect to the satellite network via serving satellites (SrvSats). As the satellites orbit the Earth at high speed, UTs and GWs frequently change their SrvSats. This causes frequent changes to their reachability, which poses a major challenge for integration. In the proposed solution, GWs and SrvSats encapsulate traffic with forwarding information so that the traffic can be carried over the satellite network towards appropriate SrvSats of UTs or GWs. The forwarding information on the encapsulating nodes is continuously updated by a controller to reflect changed SrvSats and possibly changed topology of the satellite network. Design goals for the proposed architecture were low complexity on satellites, high ability for traffic engineering, and keeping UTs out of the routing system for security and compatibility reasons. UTs may have increased security requirements (ISRs) such that their traffic should be carried within the constellation to avoid non-trusted terrestrial infrastructure. Extensions are proposed to support such ISRs. UTs may obtain either dynamic IP addresses from a nearby GW/PoP wherever they roam or they may obtain static IP addresses from a fixed Home GW/PoP. In the latter case, triangle routing via the Home GW occurs when the UT roams away from the Home GW. As this adds latency to the communication, we investigate architectural extensions for latency reduction. In addition, we show how traffic engineering can be performed in such an architecture with the help of alternate GWs and SrvSats.

papers.title: Ontology of Software Maintenance
papers.abstract: Software maintenance is often a long and costly phase of the software lifecycle, encompassing activities such as defect correction, adaptation, code improvement, and functionality enhancement. Conceptual inconsistencies and terminological variation continue to hinder effective communication among researchers and practitioners. To address this gap, this paper presents the Software Maintenance Top-Domain Ontology (SwMaintTDO), a high-domain ontology developed within a five-tier ontological architecture. This ontology was constructed using competency questions, ontological analysis of documented maintenance processes, artifacts, and resources, and alignment with established software engineering standards. SwMaintTDO provides a unified and extensible conceptual model for representing key maintenance processes, roles, resources, artifacts, goal purposes, and the transition of target modifiable and context entities from current to updated maintenance situations. The applicability and value of SwMaintTDO are demonstrated through its application -via its concepts and relationships- to the process specification of a corrective maintenance strategy.

papers.title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines
papers.abstract: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

papers.title: The Comprehension Gap in LLM-Assisted Software Development: An Experiment
papers.abstract: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. Participants needed significantly less time to solve programming tasks when working with the LLM. However, participants with high reliance on the LLM chat and low task engagement showed significantly decreased comprehension. Our qualitative results show great variability in individual perspectives on comprehension differences and strategies to mitigate issues. Strategies for dealing with comprehension differences range from accepting comprehension differences to adapting their LLM interactions or avoiding the tools altogether. Our results warrant further investigation into cognitive debt in larger systems and developer practices to mitigate issues.

papers.title: Quantifying the Intrusiveness of Retrofitting Retrieval-Augmented Generation onto Legacy Software Systems
papers.abstract: Enterprises increasingly add retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to existing REST and monolithic systems, usually by writing an ad hoc HTTP call into a handler, and have no way to quantify how intrusive that choice is. We present (1) a taxonomy of three retrofit patterns, sidecar, SDK-embed and naive-invasive; (2) the Legacy Intrusion Score (LIS), three code sub-metrics (churn, breadth, coupling), and an extension, LIS-X, with three operational sub-metrics measured on a live system (run-time overhead, fault propagation and silent feature degradation); (3) a static evaluation on five legacy systems, two of them real open-source codebases fetched from their repositories at pinned commits; and (4) a live case study that deploys all three patterns as separate OS processes. The code-level ranking sidecar < SDK-embed < naive-invasive holds in all five systems and under 2,000 random weightings, but it follows from component-wise dominance of the sub-metrics, so it validates the metric rather than testing a hypothesis. In the live study, outcomes are not fixed by definition. The sidecar adds no detectable latency to the legacy endpoint (0.07 ms, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.24]), whereas SDK-embed and naive-invasive add 569 and 475 ms and are not distinguishable from each other (p=0.62). Both pass a 2 s dependency delay on to legacy requests, and when the RAG layer fails fast they keep returning successful responses that no longer contain the AI field. Load on the RAG layer slows the legacy service by 1.51-1.57x on a shared host, and sidecar staleness averages 911 ms with a 2 s polling interval. Retrieval hit@1 is 0.95; three hosted LLMs answer all 12 test questions correctly and a local model 9/12, and the four backends are swapped by changing one request field. All dynamic results come from one host and one system.

papers.title: SWE-growth: Teacher-Guided Adaptive Self-Play for Software Engineering Agents
papers.abstract: Self-play offers a scalable way to train software engineering agents by generating repository-level repair tasks. However, with binary repair rewards and finite rollout budgets, all-fail groups provide no reward-based group-relative advantage. Such tasks may still offer learning opportunities when a Teacher can provide verified repairs absent from the Student's own attempts. We introduce SWE-Growth, a teacher-guided adaptive self-play framework that uses verified Teacher outcomes to identify learning opportunities for the current Student. Tasks with all students failure but reliable Teacher success provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and post-SFT Student rollouts identify mixed-outcome tasks with a positive Teacher--Student gap for reinforcement learning. Task eligibility also guides Injector updates, connecting Student training with subsequent task generation. Starting from 101 seed issues, \textsc{SWE-Growth} improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 27.7% to 31.7% on SWE-bench Pro and from 11.0% to 17.2% on held-out TerminalBench 2.1 by Round~2. It exceeds Student-only self-play by 2.6 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, and Teacher-augmented self-play by 1.8 and 2.5 points under approximately matched budgets. These results support adapting both supervision and task selection to the Student's evolving repair capability.

papers.title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
papers.abstract: A patch to a robot's navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path. Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches. It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong. We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits. Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task's documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them. The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks. They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis. Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.

papers.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

papers.title: What Should an LLM Know? Knowledge-Guided Warm Starts for Software Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process gigabytes in minutes; human experts work far more slowly. Prior studies that explored combinations of human/AI optimizers ignore this gap. Those studies asked systems or humans to label too many examples (e.g., SynthCore needs over four dozen per trial). Here, we test human and AI knowledge under a budget where evaluation is practical (a few dozen labels or fewer). We compare five baselines (random search, RRP, EZR, few-shot prompting, and a budget-matched SynthCore variant) against three ways to give an LLM domain knowledge before it proposes its first configurations: (1) AMP lists the domain's rules, then checks each candidate against them; (2) HKMA adds scouted data or documentation to the prompt; and (3) H-DKP has human experts correct the LLM's rules. We find that domain knowledge improves the "start-up" phase of LLM optimization, but only when that knowledge is checked, by the LLM itself or by a human expert. Across 49 datasets, unchecked knowledge did no better than few-shot prompting or EZR. On the other hand, AMP's self-checking variant (AMP-4) reached the best statistical rank in 44 of 49 datasets (budget-matched SynthCore: 23 of 49), and H-DKP did so in 7 of 8 expert studies. These checks cost little: half a cent of LLM calls per trial, or 6 to 10 expert contacts. Hence we say LLMs may not need more data, but rather their knowledge needs checking (and checking is cheap).

papers.title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
papers.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.

papers.title: YUL: Bringing Software Supply Chain Security to Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents choose and declare third-party dependencies on their own. They often declare a stale version that they recall from their training data. A stale dependency exposes the project to known vulnerabilities that the latest release already fixes. We present YUL, a design for coding agent harnesses that ensures that no stale dependencies are ever used. It does so by checking every dependency declaration against the package registry. If a dependency is stale or does not exist, YUL blocks the usage and tells the coding agent which version to use, so the coding agent retries with the fix. We evaluate YUL on 60 tasks across six ecosystems with Claude Code running Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenCode running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Without YUL, Opus declares a stale version in 29% of runs and DeepSeek in 39%, and both declare a stale version in every GitHub Actions run. With YUL, the coding agents end on the latest release in 93% of stale Opus runs and in 96% of stale DeepSeek runs. YUL thus brings the best practices of software supply chain security to coding agents.

papers.title: AppSec Core: An Ontology for Security-by-Design Software Engineering
papers.abstract: When engineers or coding agents change an application, a dependency, a configuration or a build pipeline, they need to know three things: which security rules apply, how to meet them, and what evidence to leave. Today the answers are spread over many standards, frameworks, laws and lists of weaknesses, and each one uses its own words and level of detail. This paper presents AppSec Core, a model of the security work that engineers do. It says what must be true, which practices get there, which mechanisms do the job and which artefacts show that it was done. It has 259 elements in ten domains. We built it from a security-by-design manual written from practice, and then checked it against 31 outside sources, ten of them about AI systems and agents. Along the way we made three changes, which added five objectives and made one domain wider. We did not need a new domain. Most objectives are backed by several sources: the typical objective is used by six of the twenty technical sources, and 194 of the 202 objectives, practices and mechanisms are linked to items in the sources. For the domain of a change, the model gives back a closed set of typed elements, and for a source, it gives back the objectives that the source points to. We keep the model apart from the manual, the selection rules and the server that delivers the result, and we follow one change, adding a third-party package, through all four. When a code generator received the requirements, the share of security tests passed on a public benchmark went from 77.4% to 93.0%. On a second benchmark, the result was close to that of the benchmark's own "oracle" prompt, which is written with the tests in mind.

papers.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Education for Software Developers: A Multivocal Literature Review
papers.abstract: Quantum computing threatens widely deployed public-key cryptography, making post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adoption a software engineering challenge. However, it remains unclear how well existing educational provision prepares software developers for secure PQC implementation and migration. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 8 research publications and 15 professional training offerings, examining competency coverage, practical software engineering tasks, pedagogical approaches, learner support, and evaluation. All 23 sources covered PQC foundations and algorithms, but coverage of practical software-engineering tasks was uneven. Our analysis identifies six gaps concerning developer focused evaluation, authentic software engineering tasks, task competency alignment, pedagogical design and learner support, security-focused assessment, and long term validation of learning outcomes and transfer. We derive recommendations for strengthening PQC education and better preparing software developers to implement and migrate cryptographic systems securely.

papers.title: LLMs for Software Vulnerability Prediction and Prioritization: A Review
papers.abstract: Large language models have moved beyond vulnerability detection into prediction, assessment, exploitability estimation, risk assessment and prioritization, yet the evidence for this shift has not been synthesised separately from the detection literature. In this systematic literature review, we examine how LLMs are used across those five task classes, how well they perform against established baselines, and what prevents their operational adoption. Following a prespecified protocol, we identified 197 records, removed 53 duplicates, and excluded 103 records at title and abstract stage. We assessed 41 full texts and finally retained 23 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026 after a six-question quality assessment. The review contributes a five-class taxonomy ordered by decision outcome, a method taxonomy covering prompting, tuning and retrieval or agentic architectures, an evaluation-practice audit, a bounded performance synthesis, and a deployment-barrier analysis. The main findings are that (i) assessment is the largest class (9 of 23 studies), ahead of risk assessment and prioritization (7 each); (ii) reported accuracy is highest where the label space is tightest and is not stable across evaluation periods; (iii) explanation usability is an audited evidence gap rather than a demonstrated capability; and (iv) reproducibility is the weakest reported dimension. We conclude that present systems should support analyst judgement rather than replace it, and we specify three validation studies that would settle the open questions.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play Sensor Evolution in Software-Defined Vehicles through Asset Administration Shells
papers.abstract: Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) promise continuous software evolution, but sensor integration in deployed vehicles still depends on manual configuration, hardware-specific drivers, and repeated application-side adaptation. Existing standards address only parts of this problem. AUTOSAR standardizes selected sensor interfaces, the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) standardizes signal semantics, and Asset Administration Shells (AAS) standardize digital asset descriptions. However, these building blocks are rarely combined into an end-to-end onboarding path for sensors attached after vehicle deployment. This paper presents an AAS-driven plug-and-play sensor integration framework for safety-supervised sensors. Each sensor is represented by an AAS that combines hardware identification, interface metadata, VSS mappings, and references to containerized driver and optional application software. After physical connection, an edge gateway identifies the device, retrieves the matching AAS, deploys the referenced software, and publishes the resulting data under stable vehicle signal paths. A prototype on a resource-constrained edge gateway connected to an RR100 UGV demonstrates automated integration of a USB camera and an ultrasonic sensor. Across repeated integration cycles, the prototype reaches operational state in about 2s, shows no failed events, and keeps applications independent of hardware-specific interfaces. The results indicate that the introduction of AAS as an executable onboarding contract enables automated runtime deployment of sensor drivers in SDV environments.

papers.title: From Ambiguous Tickets to Ranked Hypotheses: Multi-Agent Root-Cause Analysis for Autonomous Heavy-Vehicle Software
papers.abstract: Autonomous haulage systems run safety-critical software on driverless mining trucks, with no onboard driver to detect or mitigate abnormal behavior. Every failure in testing or operation must therefore be traced to its root cause to keep the safety case valid and limit downtime. An investigation often starts from a sparse ticket containing an approximate timestamp, sometimes a suspected cause, and a multimodal vehicle recording of several gigabytes. We present a multi-agent root-cause analysis (RCA) workflow that turns this input into a telemetry-grounded event chain, ranked causal hypotheses, and candidate code locations. A suspected cause in the ticket, which could anchor the analysis on a false theory, goes to a single LLM analyst in a separate agent session. Non-neural tools select the relevant telemetry once, before analysis, and an LLM condenses it into shared evidence artifacts; this more than halved the cost per incident compared with per-analyst querying. Specialist analyst agents then apply established RCA techniques in parallel, including fault tree analysis, Kepner-Tregoe analysis, and call-chain tracing, and hypotheses that several LLM analysts reach independently rank higher. We evaluated the workflow on 12 held-out industrial incidents against a single agent with the same model and tools. It located the faulty file more often (10 vs. 8 cases) at higher cost. Two human domain experts accepted a top-three hypothesis in 4 and 9 cases, respectively. The gap, which two LLM judges did not resolve, shows that rating causal explanations is itself a hard evaluation problem.

papers.title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
papers.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.

papers.title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
papers.abstract: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.

papers.title: An Industry Perspective on Software Vulnerability Management: A Systematic Review of Approaches, Tools, Practices, and Challenges
papers.abstract: Software vulnerability management (SVM) refers to coordinated activities to detect, assess, repair, and disclose software vulnerabilities (SVs) across a product or ecosystem. As software systems grow in scale and dependency depth, organisations must balance timely security action with limited expertise, evolving tooling, and delivery pressure. In this practitioner-centred systematic literature review, we synthesise 57 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2010 and 2025 that collect primary data directly from industry practitioners. We examine the SVM solutions (approaches, tools, and practices) proposed and evaluated with practitioners and the challenges practitioners report when adopting and using these solutions in real-world settings. We find that practice-oriented contributions, such as guidelines, recommendations, lessons learned, and shared experiences, constitute most of the evidence base, while fewer studies evaluate concrete approaches and tools in industrial environments. The solution landscape and evaluation focus are weighted toward SV detection and repair, with comparatively limited practitioner-centred coverage of SV assessment and disclosure. The most persistent challenges concern how SVM work is organised and embedded: limited security expertise and time, unclear responsibility for SV-related decisions, scattered or poorly coordinated processes, and tools that are difficult to understand, configure, or integrate into existing workflows. These findings highlight the need for more integrated socio-technical interventions, stronger coverage of under-studied SVM tasks, and evaluations that prioritise sustained workflow impact alongside technical performance.

papers.title: Escaping the Anthropomorphic Trap: Resolving the Cognitive Mismatch in Future AI Software Development
papers.abstract: For more than a half-century, the foundational paradigms of software development-such as modularity, information hiding, and hierarchical labor division-have been engineered to accommodate the strict cognitive limitations of human working memory. However, the rapid emergence of multi-agent artificial intelligence exposes a fundamental cognitive mismatch. Current frameworks attempt to integrate high-dimensional, stateless neural reasoning engines by coercing them to operate within these legacy, human-centric structures, falling into an anthropomorphic trap. This friction generates a novel, highly volatile behavioral entropy defined as AI-software technical debt, wherein amnesic agents hallucinate opaque workarounds to bypass architectural blindfolds. To resolve this, we propose Invisible Software Engineering (Invisible SE), a paradigm shift from agent-centric human emulation to environment-centric stigmergic governance. By reimagining the repository as an active computational topology which utilizes topological gradients, temporally weighted memory, and representation-space regularization, Invisible SE safely guides AI behavior without classical code-level constraints, thus transcending the cognitive horizons of human developers. This environment-centric protocol offers a potential blueprint for orchestrating scalable, long-lived computational infrastructures that transcend the cognitive horizons of human developers and enable autonomous agents to work, coordinate, and scale to build future software systems.

papers.title: Software Engineering for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based Agents perform tasks through tool use and interaction with external environments. Public engineering guidance commonly begins with a target task, selects a suitable workflow or autonomous Agent design, and refines prompts, tools, and execution strategies using task outcomes, latency, and cost. When delivered as software systems, Agents must also satisfy stakeholder requirements, action boundaries, quality checks, and maintenance needs. Model-directed execution can vary across runs, failures can span model decisions and tools, and changes to prompts, models, or interfaces can affect previously accepted behavior. This survey examines how LLM-based Agents are engineered across five software lifecycle stages: Requirements Engineering, Architecture and Design, Implementation and Integration, Testing and Assurance, and Maintenance and Evolution. Based on a main collection of 355 papers, we compare the engineering problems addressed, explain how methods and practices work, and examine their reported evaluations and limitations within each stage. We synthesize how existing research supports Agent development activities and identify open problems and research directions. The result is a lifecycle-oriented reference for understanding, selecting, and further developing methods for engineering Agent software.

papers.title: Exploring Students' Insights on Creating Videos to Learn Software Design and Engineering
papers.abstract: This research-to-practice study examines the use of student-created instructional videos as an active learning strategy in a large undergraduate Software Design and Engineering (SWE) course. Supporting engagement and understanding in large-scale computer science (CS) courses remains a challenge, as instruction often relies on automated activities and summative assessments that prioritize grading over meaningful learning. This can make the learning experience feel impersonal, leading to frustration, anxiety, and confusion, especially when students face complex topics or new programming tools. To address these issues, we implemented a learner-centered strategy grounded in the principle of ``learning by teaching," where students created instructional videos to explain course concepts in their own words. This approach allowed students to take ownership of their learning, adapting the material to fit their individual perspectives and reinforcing their understanding through explanation. We report on students' reflections from a large introductory SWE course (over 700 students), analyzing their open-ended feedback on the benefits and drawbacks of the strategy. Students highlighted increased engagement and learning, and many appreciated the flexibility of the video-based format compared to traditional multiple-choice exams, which they found more restrictive. However, students also noted that the video creation process was time-consuming. This study contributes to the growing conversation on active learning in computing and engineering education by showcasing the potential of student-created instructional videos to enhance student agency, motivation, and conceptual understanding in large-scale learning environments.

papers.title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
papers.abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

papers.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
papers.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

papers.title: Trustworthy Numerical Software in the Age of AI: What Would Turing Do?
papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now produce numerical software faster than human experts can review it, raising serious concerns about usability and reliability. These and other AI tools are already transforming mathematics and software, and they will soon transform mathematical software. These concerns motivated us to assess AI-generated numerical linear algebra (NLA) kernels, which we did through an audit of a recent public GPU QR competition. All five leading kernels passed the competition's accuracy tests, and the winning kernel achieved a 107-fold speedup over the competition's baseline, which calls NVIDIA's QR routine. Yet each failed at least once on new inputs, even those from the competition's generator, under the same checker, while the baseline passed them all. In light of this, we want to develop reusable formalizations of numerical analysis methods, which remain sparsely represented in existing formal libraries. We describe VSCL, our Lean library of mathematical foundations for numerical computing. We also propose VERNA to connect these tasks by using formalized results to guide kernel assessment against explicit specifications. Drawing on Turing's work on rounding-error analysis and program checking, we discuss design principles for developing trustworthy numerical software when direct human checking is impractical.

papers.title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints
papers.abstract: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out. Leaderboard ranks give weak evidence for this decision. Accuracy differences may be statistically unresolved, reported costs may be inconsistent, and evaluating candidate agents can itself be expensive. We investigate budget-constrained agent selection using 58,197 run--task records extracted from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), focusing on SWE-bench and six additional benchmarks. Across seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy--cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved. On SWE-bench, a run costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, but the available tasks cannot statistically distinguish their accuracy. Reported costs also differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7x, while selective task evaluation can bias estimates of full-benchmark execution cost. We therefore compare evaluation strategies under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment-cost caps. Under advance knowledge of task costs, successive halving reaches our uncertainty-aware selection target on SWE-bench using 6.6% of exhaustive evaluation spend, achieving the lowest cost on six of seven benchmarks and tying on the seventh. Its advantage narrows when task costs are unknown before execution or exact-best selection is required. Our findings motivate decision-oriented agent evaluation that accounts for accuracy uncertainty, validates execution costs, and compares complex selection methods against simple adaptive allocation.

papers.title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
papers.abstract: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

papers.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
